messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 44
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Nurse
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 68

He shows up for his shift a half-hour early now, even though the locker room is still empty and the fluorescent lights buzz alone. He needs that extra time to walk every hallway first, to check the stairwell doors, to scan the parking lot from the third-floor window. He knows it doesn’t make sense—the mugging happened three blocks from the hospital, not inside it—but his chest doesn’t care what his mind knows.

It was a Tuesday night, eleven months ago. He had just finished a double shift in the ICU, too tired to wait for the bus, so he started walking toward the train. The streets were quiet, wet from earlier rain. He remembers the smell of fried noodles from a cart, the way his scrubs clung to his back. A man stepped out from behind a dumpster, asked for his wallet. He handed it over. Then another man appeared, and there was a knife, and then he was on the ground, and the knife was at his throat, and he heard himself say, *“Please, I have a wife.”* They took his phone, his watch, his badge. Left him bleeding from a small cut on his jaw.

He went to work the next day. He didn’t tell anyone. Not his supervisor, not his wife. He thought if he just kept moving, it would dissolve. But it didn’t.

Now, when a patient’s monitor beeps too fast, his hands shake. When a visitor stands too close to him at the nurses’ station, his peripheral vision narrows. Last week, an elderly man with dementia grabbed his arm during a wound dressing, and he jerked away so violently he knocked a tray of supplies to the floor. He apologized, said he was startled. The patient didn’t remember, but he does.

He avoids the stairwells. He takes the elevator even if it means waiting five minutes. He has not walked to the train station since that night. His wife drives him to work now, or he takes a rideshare. She asked once why he stopped riding the bus, and he said he was saving time. She knows he is lying. She has asked him to talk to someone, but he says, “I’m fine, I’m a nurse, I’ve seen worse.” And he has. He has held dying patients, cleaned wounds that would make most people faint. But this is different. This is the feeling of his own pulse backing up into his throat every time he hears footsteps behind him, even in his own home, even when it’s just his wife coming into the kitchen.

At night, he wakes up in a cold sweat, sometimes not even sure what he dreamed—just a flash of concrete, a glint of metal, the sound of his own voice begging. He lies still beside his wife, counting her breaths, forcing himself to stay in the room. But he doesn’t sleep again.

At work, he is quieter now. The other nurses notice. He used to joke with the families, used to stay late to chat with the night crew. Now he keeps his head down, follows his rounds, and leaves the moment his shift ends. He cannot stand the feeling of being watched. He has started wearing his watch on his right wrist instead of his left, because the watch that was taken was on his left, and seeing that empty space still makes his stomach seize.

He knows something is wrong. He scored a 68 on that questionnaire the clinic gave him—he looked it up online. But knowing the number doesn’t bring back the feeling of being safe. It only gives him a name for the thing that has taken up residence behind his sternum. He arrives early, leaves quickly, sleeps poorly, and trusts no one. He is a good nurse. But he is not the same man.
